claim: MonoTrack reconstructs 3D shuttle trajectories from monocular video by modeling the shuttle as a particle under quadratic air drag, with a drag coefficient that can change per shot, plus court and shot-placement priors. On 10k synthetic trajectories the priors cut the average 3D error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm. Real matches have no 3D ground truth, so only 2D reprojection error was measured: 8.1-9.8 px bootstrapped and up to 37.1 px end-to-end (about 5% of image resolution).
quote: On average, adding the priors improves the error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm. ... The highest error is 37.1 pixels, or about 5% given the image resolution we are working with.

verifier_notes.evidence:
I checked every part of the claim against the primary source, the arXiv HTML of 2204.01899 (Liu & Wang, "MonoTrack: Shuttle trajectory reconstruction from monocular badminton video", CVSports@CVPR 2022, DOI 10.1109/CVPRW56347.2022.00395).

(1) **Physics model:** Section 4.5 models the shuttle as "a particle under drag". Eq. 1 is d²x/dt² = g − C_d‖x‖₂x. The paper writes x where velocity is meant, which is a typo; read with velocity, this is velocity-squared (quadratic) drag. The paper never uses the word "quadratic", but the description is accurate. It also says: "Note C_d can change from shot to shot, as the shuttlecock feathers slowly break over the course of a rally." So the per-shot drag coefficient is supported.

(2) **Priors:** The priors are the hitter and receiver positions, estimated from their feet at a 2 m height, plus an out-of-court penalty d_O. Calling these "court and shot-placement priors" is a fair summary.

(3) **Synthetic test:** The paper says "an additional evaluation dataset containing 10k synthetic trajectories" and "On average, adding the priors improves the error from 14.9 cm to 8.0 cm". The metric is the distance between the true and reconstructed 3D trajectories. The numbers match exactly.

(4) **Real matches:** The paper states that "3D ground truth positions are not available and thus only 2D reprojection error can be computed". Table 2 gives bootstrapped errors of 8.1, 8.9 and 9.8 px and end-to-end errors of 37.1, 28.8 and 23.3 px, plus the quote "The highest error is 37.1 pixels, or about 5% given the image resolution". So "8.1-9.8 px bootstrapped, up to 37.1 px end-to-end" is exact.

The claim does not overreach. It says the 3D error comes only from synthetic data and that real matches have only 2D reprojection error. The source is primary and peer-reviewed at a CVPR workshop, and it is not marketing.

A web search found no follow-up paper that disputes these numbers. The paper is from 2022, but the claim only describes what MonoTrack reported, not that it is the best method in 2026. Its age matters for the wider research question, not for whether this claim is true.

Minor caveats: the synthetic test adds ±0.5 m uniform noise to the 3D hit positions, but the paper does not describe any noise on the 2D observations. That means the 8.0 cm figure is probably optimistic compared with real-world 3D accuracy. The claim's own wording already hedges this.

A derivative-based hit detector, which works much like the app's current velocity-peak thresholding, gets F1 0.699 on the same test set. HitNet without the optimization step reaches F1 0.866.

All the numbers match the primary source. I checked arXiv 2204.01899v2 (Liu & Wang, May 18 2022), which was published at the peer-reviewed CVSports@CVPR 2022 workshop (doi:10.1109/CVPRW56347.2022.00395). Its Table 1 columns are recall/acc./prec./F1, and the rows read exactly as quoted:
- Derivative-based: 65.7% / 53.8% / 74.7% / 0.699
- HitNet (All): 78.1% / 76.4% / 97.2% / 0.866
- HitNet+optimization: 94.3% / 89.7% / 94.9% / 0.946
Other ablation rows are RF 0.730, HitNet (Shuttle) 0.815 and HitNet (Shuttle+Pose) 0.850. Section 4.4 confirms "around 16K parameters" and per-frame inputs of court corners, both players' poses and the shuttle location. These go through a 32-dim embedding and 2 GRU layers over 12-frame windows.

Problems that qualify the claim but do not refute it:
(a) The comparison to the app is overstated. MonoTrack's derivative baseline "detects a hit when the second derivative of either the shuttle x-coordinate or y-coordinate exceeds a predefined threshold." That is shuttle acceleration, not the wrist-velocity peak the app uses. The 0.699 score therefore does not directly predict how the app's detector performs.
(b) The sequence optimization is effectively offline. It uses rally duration to set the expected hit count (about 1 hit/s), a minimum 0.5 s gap between hits, alternating hitters, and dynamic programming over the whole sequence. So the 0.946 is not achievable in real time.
(c) Evaluation is on 12k frames from 3 test matches of the TrackNetV2 broadcast dataset (26 international singles matches). That is fixed broadcast footage, not phone video.
(d) The paper's text reports "86.3% accuracy" for HitNet, but Table 1 gives 76.4%. This is an internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim.
(e) The paper is from 2022, but the claim only reports these numbers and does not call them state of the art.

No source contradicts the figures. Hsu et al. (Sensors 2024, PMC11244353) report F1 90.5% for TrackNet + YOLOv7 + shot refinement on 69 BWF matches, but on different data, so the two are not directly comparable.

Here xH and xR are hit and receive positions taken from the players' feet, with a 2 m height. dO penalises trajectories that land outside the court. There are also hard constraints: height ≤3 m, speed ≤120 m/s, the shot starts on the hitter's side, and initial velocity points toward the opponent. Calling these "court and shot-placement priors" fairly matches the abstract's wording ("court dimension, shot placement, physical laws of motion").

claim: Court calibration needs no homography or keypoint detection. The user clicks two points on a court line at the same depth as the impact point, and the system computes one meters-per-pixel scale factor (S_f = d_real / d_pixel). 1. **Method.** Calibration is manual and uses no homography or keypoint detection. The user picks two points on a court line, such as the rear doubles line or front service line. That line must be parallel to the camera's image plane and at the same distance from the camera as the impact point. The scale factor is S_f = d_real / d_pixel in meters per pixel. Speed is pixel displacement per frame × S_f × 3.6, and the peak value is reported.
2. **2D assumption.** The paper says the camera must be "perpendicular to the shuttlecock's primary plane of motion" and that "This orthogonal viewpoint effectively eliminates the z-axis (depth) from calculations."

The limitation also follows from basic geometry: a single meters-per-pixel scale cannot capture motion in depth. MonoTrack (CVPRW 2022, arXiv 2204.01899) avoids it by reconstructing 3D trajectories from court dimensions and physics, which is consistent with the paper's own view that 2D scaling is limited.

- The first sentence, "Court calibration needs no homography or keypoint detection," is accurate only as a description of this one system. It is not general advice, and the paper itself frames the 2D approach as a limitation, with 3D reconstruction listed as future work.

In hit/move.py, calc_ground_projection averages COCO keypoints 15 and 16 (the left and right ankles). road/position.py builds the plane normal as cross(hit2 - hit1, [0,0,1]) and computes compute_air_point by ray-plane intersection.

There are two small qualifications, neither of which overturns the claim:
(a) The anchor is not literally at the ankle midpoint. The paper itself says "feet"; the code uses ankle keypoints.
(b) The paper describes the plane as "approximately orthogonal" to the court and the anchor as a heuristic. If there is no second strike, the landing point is used as the second anchor.

The claim makes no benchmark numbers, so the self-reported 170 cm to 7.8 cm landing-error result has no bearing on it. I found no contradicting source.

claim: MonoTrack's modified TrackNetV2 shuttle tracker raises tracking accuracy from 84.0% to 88.6% while shrinking the model from 11.3M to 2.9M parameters. Input is 288x512 and the model predicts three frames at once. No precision, recall or F1 is reported for this tracker.

verifier_notes.evidence:
I'm marking this refuted because a credible independent evaluation heavily qualifies it, even though it accurately repeats the MonoTrack paper. The final sentence is also wrong if read as covering the literature generally.

What the primary source supports: Section 4.3 of the MonoTrack paper (Liu & Wang, arXiv 2204.01899, CVSports@CVPR 2022) does state "88.6% accuracy from 84.0% in the original" and "2.9M parameters in our model versus 11.3M parameters". It also describes 288x512 input, a 3-in-3-out design, residual connections, and a dice + BCE loss. The paper reports no precision, recall or F1 for the shuttle tracker, and it never defines tracking accuracy or ties the 84.0/88.6 figures to a test split. These numbers are self-reported.

Why it is refuted:
(1) WASB (Tarashima et al., arXiv 2311.05237, BMVC 2023) re-implemented both models and ran them on the same badminton data at a 4-pixel distance threshold (Table 2). The results were:
- TrackNetV2: 11.3M params, F1 90.5, Acc 85.6, AP 83.6
- MonoTrack: 2.9M params, F1 90.9, Acc 85.9, AP 84.9
The independent gain is about +0.3 accuracy points, not the claimed +4.6. Presenting "raises tracking accuracy from 84.0% to 88.6%" as a benchmark fact therefore overstates MonoTrack's advantage.
(2) "No precision, recall or F1 is reported for this tracker" is only true of the MonoTrack paper itself. WASB reports F1 90.9 and AP 84.9 for MonoTrack, so the statement is misleading for a research question that asks for published benchmark numbers.
(3) A web search summary says the TrackNetV2 paper itself reported 85.2% on its test match, not 84.0%, which would suggest MonoTrack re-ran its own baseline. I could not confirm this from the TrackNetV2 paper.
(4) Both models are superseded on this benchmark. WASB scores F1 93.1 / Acc 89.0 with 1.5M params in Step=1 mode, and TrackNetV3 (2023) has also been released.

The parameter counts (11.3M and 2.9M) and the architecture details hold up in both sources. The accuracy-gain framing and the "no F1" statement do not survive independent checking.

2. **Precision went down.** It fell from 96.6 to 94.9, and false positives rose: FP1 from 438 to 765, FP2 from 493 to 672. The F1 gain is exactly 0.8 points, not "over 0.8%".

2. **The data split differs.** The V5 paper uses a 7:3 train/validation split with no separate test split described. Its figures are therefore not directly comparable to V3's test-split numbers.
3. **The V4 baseline contradicts other sources.** In this paper V4 scores below V2 (Acc 0.9224 vs 0.9396).
   - The V4 paper itself (arXiv 2409.14543) reports V4 improving on V2 (F1 90.6 to 91.4) and on V3 (97.5 to 97.9).

4. **The name is ambiguous.** The NYCU paper above is a different "TrackNetV5" (R(2+1)D, motion prompts, SCG fusion). It reports its own SOTA claim: F1 98.47, Acc 97.37, P 99.72, R 97.25. It also has a Lite variant (2.58M parameters, F1 98.06), which is more relevant for on-device use.
5. **The paper's own ablation undercuts the headline.** Table 5 shows V2 + R-STR alone at F1 0.9866 / Acc 0.9745, higher than the full V5 at 0.9859 / 0.9733.
6. **Source quality is limited.** It is an arXiv preprint with no venue confirmed. Benchmark numbers on this dataset vary widely by protocol: V2's F1 ranges from 90.6 to 97.03 to 96.77 across papers.

CONCLUSION
The numbers are what the paper says, but presenting this model as the clear SOTA that "beats V2 and V4" is an overreach. The comparison leaves out TrackNetV3, which matches or exceeds it on the same dataset.

claim: A smartphone badminton smash-speed system that combines a custom YOLOv5 shuttle detector with a linear constant-velocity Kalman filter (a SORT-style setup, close to Ayto's current YOLOv8n+KF approach) produced peak speeds far from radar: MAE 66.41 km/h and RMSE 74.68 km/h over 20 smashes filmed on an iPhone 16 at 30 FPS against a Bushnell Speedster III radar. The system's peak readings ran well above radar in every trial (for example, 214.6 vs 132.0 km/h).
quote: The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) between the two methods for peak speed was 66.41 km/h, and the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) was 74.68 km/h.

verifier_notes.evidence:
I'm marking this claim refuted. The quoted numbers are real, but the claim reads them in a way the source rejects.

What the claim gets right (checked against arXiv 2509.05334v1, Diwen Huang, independent researcher, submitted 1 Sep 2025):
- The setup matches the claim: custom YOLOv5 detector, linear constant-velocity Kalman filter "similar to SORT", iPhone 16 at 30 FPS, Bushnell Speedster III radar, 20 smashes.
- Section 4.3 does report peak-speed MAE 66.41 km/h and RMSE 74.68 km/h.
- In Table 1 the system's peak is above the radar in all 20 trials (e.g., 214.6 vs 132.0, 261.2 vs 119.0).

Why I count it as a misread:
1. The claim treats the gap as a system failure. The author says the opposite: "This large difference does not indicate an error in our system." The paper puts the gap down to aerodynamic drag slowing the shuttle. It says the radar needs the shuttle to travel some distance before it locks on, so it is "physically incapable of capturing" peak velocity. The peak-vs-radar comparison sets two different quantities against each other.
2. The like-for-like comparison is left out. Table 1 also gives the system's "At Net" speed. Recomputed from that table, at-net vs radar gives MAE 9.9 km/h, RMSE 13.2 km/h and a mean bias of +2.5 km/h, with readings on both sides of the radar. The author uses this agreement to argue the system is "calibrated correctly". So for "accuracy vs radar", the relevant number is about 10 km/h, not 66 km/h.
3. The headline figures don't match the paper's own table. Recomputing peak-vs-radar from Table 1 gives MAE 69.41 and RMSE 76.36, not 66.41 / 74.68.
4. The source is weak for any claim about how accurate this approach is. It is a single-author arXiv preprint with no sign of peer review and only 20 smashes from one player. Smashes were deliberately kept below full power because of the radar's limits. Nothing measures the true peak speed, so the peak values are neither confirmed nor shown to be wrong.

As written, the claim would lead the synthesis to say a YOLO+Kalman phone speed system has about 66 km/h error against radar. The source does not support that.
